passage: I'm Meena from next door, and on Saturday I watched Jahnavi and Harish turn their living room into a quiz hall. Harish's father read out questions from a card, and Jahnavi's mother held up a steel spoon. "First to grab the spoon answers!" Harish grabbed it three times in a row. Jahnavi got the science questions, and Harish the sports ones. By the end, they had a small tally on the wall. "I am slow on history," Jahnavi admitted. "And I miss geography," said Harish. They wrote both on a sticky note. I had thought it was just a game, but I saw it was a test with a purpose.

qa.q: What did the parents use as a buzzer?
qa.a: They used a steel spoon as a buzzer.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi and Harish feel about their weak topics, and what shows it?
qa.a: They seemed comfortable and honest, not embarrassed, admitting history and geography aloud and writing both on a sticky note.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the pair use to prepare, and why?
qa.a: They could split the subjects between them and each become the expert. That would save time and reduce clashes over answers.

qa.q: How does Meena see the mock quiz?
qa.a: Meena thought it was just a game and then saw it was a purposeful test, so Meena's view changed to respect for how seriously the two were preparing.

grounding: A team of two asks parents to read questions with a spoon as a buzzer, and the practice shows who answers fastest and which topics are weak.

Sunday: Jatin and Ira were a two-person quiz team, and the school contest was in three weeks. They asked Ira's parents to read out questions from an old quiz book after lunch. Ira's father handed them each a steel spoon. "Bang the plate, that's your buzzer."
Wednesday: Round two at Jatin's house, with his mother reading. They kept score on a sheet. Jatin was faster on sports. Ira was faster on science. Neither of them buzzed on anything about rivers or capitals.
Saturday: They looked at the score sheet together. "Geography," Ira said. "We're both bad at it." They drew up a plan: one map a day each, and a spoon round every Sunday.

qa.q: What did Ira's father give them to use as buzzers?
qa.a: He gave each of them a steel spoon.

qa.q: How did Ira feel when she saw the geography gap on the score sheet?
qa.a: She seemed calm and determined, naming the weak area plainly and turning it into a plan.

qa.q: What else could Jatin and Ira do with the scores they now have?
qa.a: They could split the questions by strength in the real contest, with Jatin leading sports and Ira science.

qa.q: How does the practice look to the parents reading the questions?
qa.a: The parents seem to enjoy it, making a game of it with spoons and plates.

grounding: It shows a pair of friends using mock rounds read by parents, with spoons as buzzers, to learn who answers fastest and what topics are weak.

passage: Omkar, you want to know how your Lalit Dada won the Class 5 quiz? Not with luck. My friend Joseph and I made a plan. We couldn't buy a buzzer, so we used my mother's steel spoons and the thali. Every evening for two weeks, my father sat on the charpai with the question book and read, and we banged the thali when we knew. Whoever banged first answered. Oh, the noise! The neighbours complained. But by the third evening we knew something. Joseph was quicker on science. I was quicker on cricket. And both of us were hopeless on world capitals. So we spent the last week on capitals only. In the final, the last question was a capital. We banged together.

qa.q: What did Lalit and Joseph use as a buzzer?
qa.a: They used steel spoons and the thali.

qa.q: How did young Lalit feel when the last question in the final was a capital?
qa.a: Young Lalit must have felt excited and ready, since the pair had spent the last week on capitals.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Noticing on the third evening that both were weak on capitals mattered most, because it told them exactly what to practise.

qa.q: How might Lalit's father have seen those noisy evenings?
qa.a: The father probably found them tiring but enjoyable, and was proud when the practice paid off.

grounding: An elder recalls, as a boy, practising with a friend in mock rounds read by his father with spoons for buzzers, which showed who was fastest and what was weak.
